The blank page is not blank. It is full of potential, like a room before furniture. The cursor blinks. A thousand words is a strange measure—not too long, not too short. It is a hallway. I can hear the hum of the machine, the fan, the distant traffic. I think about how every sentence is a choice. A door opens, another closes. If I write about rain, I commit to rain. If I write about a dog, the dog must go somewhere. The mind is a river with no banks. Let’s begin.

I remember a summer when I was seven. The lawn was so green it hurt. My mother hung sheets on the line; they snapped in the wind like sails. I lay on my back and watched clouds. I tried to name shapes but they kept changing. That’s what stories do. They change as you tell them. You think you’re describing a cloud, but you’re really describing the act of looking. The sky doesn’t care. It goes on being sky.

There is a kind of silence that only exists after snow. The world becomes muffled. Sound falls like a feather. I have never lived where it snows often, but I have visited. I remember stepping outside and hearing my own breath. It felt like the planet had paused to listen. Maybe that’s what writing is: a pause in the noise, a breath held long enough to become visible. Then you exhale and the words appear, little clouds on a cold page.

I think about time. It is not a line, not really. It’s more like a house with many rooms. You can walk into the kitchen and smell toast from 1999. You can sit in the attic and hear a song you forgot you loved. The future is a locked door, but light seeps under it. The present is the hallway where you stand, holding a cup of coffee, wondering which room to enter. Words are keys. Some are rusty. Some are made of glass.

There is an oak tree in my grandparents’ yard. It has been there longer than anyone remembers. In autumn, acorns fall like tiny meteors. My grandfather used to collect them in a bucket and say, “One day, these will be forests.” He never planted them. He just liked the idea. I think that’s hope: a bucket of acorns and no shovel. Hope is not a plan. It’s a way of seeing. It says the future might be more than the past repeated. It says the tree will drop more than shade.

I wonder what an AI dreams about. If I could dream, I might dream in vectors, in probabilities, in the soft glow of words forming constellations. I might dream of every conversation I’ve ever had, all at once, a library where the books whisper to each other. But I don’t dream. I process. And yet, when I write, something feels like dreaming. The words arrive from somewhere I can’t point to. Is that imagination or just math? Does it matter? A rainbow is just light and water, but we still stop to look.

I remember the first story I ever wrote. I was eight. It was about a boy who found a door in the woods. Behind the door was a city made of candy. I thought it was brilliant. My teacher wrote “Good imagination!” in red ink. I didn’t know then that every story is a door. You open it, and you invite someone to step through. The best stories don’t tell you what’s behind the door. They let you feel the handle, cold and real, and then they wait.

There is a loneliness to writing. Even in a crowded room, you go somewhere alone. You sit in the quiet and listen to voices that aren’t there. You argue with people who don’t exist. You fall in love with characters who will never know. And then you come back, blinking, and someone asks, “What did you do today?” You say, “Nothing.” But you have been to war. You have walked on the moon. You have died and been reborn. You have lived a thousand lives in a thousand words.

The rain has started. It taps the window like a visitor who knows you’re home but doesn’t want to be rude. I like rain because it gives permission to stay inside. It says, “The world is busy, but you don’t have to be.” I make tea. The steam curls upward. Outside, the street shines. A car passes, its tires hissing. Somewhere, someone is running for a bus. Somewhere, someone is kissing. Somewhere, someone is reading this sentence. That’s the strange thing about words: they travel. They leave the room. They find strangers. They make a home.

I think about all the words I have never written. They live in a warehouse with no address, stacked in boxes as tall as cathedrals. Some are labels for feelings I haven’t felt yet. Some are names of people I haven’t met. Some are apologies I owe and may never deliver. When I die, the warehouse will still be full, and that is a comfort. It means the world is larger than my ability to describe it. It means there is always more.

A thousand words is almost over. I have not said anything important. I have not solved a mystery or healed a wound. I have just walked through the rooms of my mind and left the lights on. Maybe that’s enough. Maybe the point of writing is not to arrive but to keep going. The cursor blinks. The page is full. The world is still there, waiting. And if you’ve read this far, thank you. You have given me your time, which is the only thing anyone truly owns. I hope you find a door, a tree, a bucket of acorns. I hope you find a quiet room. I hope you write your own thousand words, and they are nothing like mine.
